problem: Existing memory-based image-goal navigation methods focus on exploitation (finding the target from memory) and neglect designing exploratory behavior. Online-built implicit scene representations such as NeRF are noisy early in an episode and give little useful memory.
motivation: Robots in unknown scenes must first explore to build cognition, then exploit it to reach the target. Uncertainty of an online NeRF marks unexplored regions, so it can drive exploration and speed up building the representation, while NeRF-derived spatial features support target reasoning.
key_idea: Use an online-trained NeRF with per-ray uncertainty as the memory. Render an uncertainty map for exploratory features and a spatial feature map for exploitative features, then adaptively fuse both with perceptual features to output actions end-to-end.
insight: Uncertainty features alone improve the total SR from 36.48% (no f_u, no AT, no CBAM) to 43.53%. Removing f_u from the full model drops SR to 46.25% versus 59.65%, so uncertainty is the largest contributor. Grad-CAM shows the policy attends to high-uncertainty regions, and the auxiliary direction-prediction accuracy rises after the target is seen, which indicates a natural exploration-to-exploitation transition.
method: Online cognition generation: an ActiveNeRF-style NeRF is trained online, with a Gaussian radiance model (mean and variance) and a heteroscedastic NLL loss, giving per-point uncertainty.
Exploratory thinking: the uncertainty is volume-rendered into a map I_u, compressed by ResNet blocks and CBAM (channel and spatial attention) into a 64-d feature f_u.

Exploitative thinking: intermediate NeRF features are volume-rendered into a 64-channel spatial map I_cog, concatenated with the target image, then passed through ResNet, CBAM and an MLP into a 64-d f_cog.
Auxiliary task: a two-layer MLP predicts the angle between the robot heading and the target direction from f_cog, trained with L1 loss for interpretability and better reasoning.

Multi-thinking integration: f_cog, f_u and a real-time perceptual feature f_p are concatenated, an attention MLP produces weights, and the reweighted feature goes to an MLP policy that samples a discrete action.
Training: imitation learning, end-to-end and differentiable, with the NeRF built online during each episode.

setting.backbone: ResNet + CBAM + MLP policy with an online-trained ActiveNeRF-style NeRF (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: Imitation learning on Gibson scenes in iGibson (21 training scenes, 14 validation scenes)
setting.privileged: none stated at test time (training uses ground-truth target direction for the auxiliary loss and imitation supervision)

numbers.extra: Total across Easy/Medium/Hard; max 800 steps; success radius 0.8 m; SR is printed as a percentage and SPL as a fraction
numbers.evidence: Table I 'Image-goal navigation results', row Ours, Total

numbers.extra: ablation variant (f_u and CBAM kept, AT removed)
numbers.evidence: Table I ablation row (f_u ✓, AT ✗, CBAM ✓), Total

numbers_note: Custom iGibson image-goal benchmark; the 14 Gibson 'validation' scenes are used for testing, so the split label 'val' is an approximation. Easy and Medium results are also in the table but not listed here.
results: NUE reaches 59.65% total SR, 0.385 SPL and 2.053 DTS. It beats memory-based baselines VGM (41.37%), MSM and NRNS, and beats SLING+OVRL (56.64% SR, 0.379 SPL) on total SR, and on Hard SR (54.75% vs 51.75%). SLING+OVRL still has higher SPL on Easy and Medium.
limitations: Evaluated only in simulation (iGibson/Gibson) on a custom split, with no real-robot experiments
Online NeRF training and rendering are computationally heavy, and the paper reports no efficiency analysis
Compared against a limited set of baselines; SLING+OVRL still has better Easy and Medium SPL
